_comment: Registration for scripts/undeclared-import-audit.py (issue #1041).
WHY THIS GATE NEEDS A COMMITTED CASE (ADR 0008): it is a gate that lets work
THROUGH. `make verify` and the CI `undeclared-import-audit` step both read its
green as 'no module-level import in this tree resolves to a distribution nothing
declares', and nothing downstream re-derives that. A blind version prints the
identical clean line over the pre-#1041 tree, where three files had imported three
undeclared packages since the initial commit and no instrument in the repository
could see any of them - `[tool.mypy] ignore_missing_imports = true`, and ruff's
selected rules (E, F, W, I) do not check that an import is declared.
THE CASES ARE WHOLE FIXTURE TREES, not the real repository. The gate takes
--root and --allow-file, so a case is a miniature project: a `pyproject.toml`, a
little Python, and its own ledger. Deliberately tiny - the question is whether the
gate can tell a declared tree from an undeclared one, not whether it can read 274
files.
STDLIB-ONLY AND OFFLINE, which is what makes these valid where the harness runs.
The `negative-controls` CI step runs a bare `python3` with no `uv sync`, so a case
needing an installed package or the network would report UNSIGNALLED there - an
environment failure wearing the diagnosis 'the gate stopped discriminating'. This
gate reads committed metadata only and never the ambient environment (that refusal
is the point of its resolution order, and is why it needs no captures the way
controls/dependency-audit and controls/bandit-audit do).
THREE BAD CASES, because the gate draws three distinctions and a control that
exercises one leaves the others unproven:
bad-stub-only-declaration     THE CASE ISSUE #1041 IS ABOUT, reproduced. The
type STUBS are declared (`types-requests`) and the
package is not, so the name a careless matcher
looks for is present in the metadata while the
dependency is absent. This is why the declaration
test is an exact compare of PEP-503-normalized
names and not a substring search - and it is
precisely what the anchor below misses.
bad-second-import-unaccounted a file with TWO undeclared imports and a ledger
line accepting ONE. Without it, a gate that keyed
acceptance on the FILE rather than the (file,
import name) pair would pass: one recorded
exception would silently accept every future
undeclared import added to the same file, which is
how a per-file suppression quietly becomes a
per-file blindfold.
bad-stale-allow               a CLEAN tree beside a ledger line accounting for
nothing - the state a tree enters the moment
someone FIXES a recorded site. The forward check
alone scores that tree clean, so without this case
the ledger accumulates lines recording nothing and
nobody is told. This direction is the whole reason
the ledger is not a `--skip`, which has no
direction in which it can go stale.
THIS CASE EARNED ITS PLACE ON THE FIRST RUN, which is recorded because a control
that has never fired is a claim rather than evidence. #1041 intended to record
`woodpecker/bootstrap-secrets.py` importing boto3 as an accepted entry. The same
change declared boto3 as the `aws` extra for `lib/creds/providers/aws.py`, which
resolved that import too - and the stale direction reported the entry as accounting
for nothing the first time the gate ran. The ledger caught its own author writing a
false record, and the entry was deleted rather than kept.
TWO GOOD CASES, and the second is not redundant:
good-all-declared             every legitimate reason an import is NOT a finding,
in one tree: stdlib, a first-party package, a
first-party module reached through a `sys.path`
insert of a local `src/` dir (the delivery-pilot
shape, which a naive scan reports as two
third-party findings), an alias (`yaml` ships as
the distribution `pyyaml`), a package declared in
an EXTRA rather than in `dependencies`, an import
inside a function body, one guarded by an
ImportError handler, and one under `if
TYPE_CHECKING:` which never executes. THE HALF
THAT MATTERS for a gate wedged at 'fail': the bad
cases alone cannot tell a working gate from one
that refuses everything, and this gate is in `make
verify`, so a false red blocks every merge in the
repository.
good-allowed-accounted        the ledger's ACCEPT direction, which no bad case
proves. `bad-second-import-unaccounted` still
scores BAD under a gate that ignores the ledger
entirely (it would simply report two findings
instead of one), so without this case the accept
path could be dead code and every registered case
would still pass.
WHAT THESE CASES DO NOT ESTABLISH, said plainly: that the gate is ever pointed at
the real tree, or that its population is the one we meant. A case supplies its own
root. That half is covered by `undeclared-import-audit.py --selftest`, which runs
the real code path over two committed trees under `live/` - one holding a planted
module-level `import requests` it must report, one clean it must not - and which
`make verify` and the CI step both run BEFORE the real audit, so no clean verdict
is issued by a scan that was never shown able to find something. Neither half is
sufficient alone; naming which one covers which is the point.

cases.name: bad-stub-only-declaration
cases.why: A module-level `import requests` in a tree whose only related declaration is `types-requests`, the type stubs. If this scores GOOD the gate cannot see the exact state issue #1041 was filed against, which is the only state it was built for. The anchor reports it clean, because `types-requests` contains the substring `requests`.

cases.name: bad-second-import-unaccounted
cases.why: Two undeclared module-level imports in one file, with a ledger line accepting one of them. If this scores GOOD, acceptance is keyed on the FILE and a single recorded exception silently accepts every undeclared import added to that file afterwards. The anchor reports it clean: both names appear in the metadata as `types-` prefixed stubs.

cases.name: bad-stale-allow
cases.why: A clean tree beside a ledger line that accounts for nothing - what a tree looks like the moment a recorded site is FIXED. If this scores GOOD the ledger can accumulate lines recording nothing, which is how an allowlist decays into a permanent blindfold. The anchor has no stale direction at all, so it reports clean.

cases.name: good-all-declared
cases.why: Every legitimate non-finding in one tree: stdlib, first-party package, first-party module behind a sys.path insert, the `yaml`/`pyyaml` alias, an extra-only declaration, a function-body import, an ImportError-guarded import, and a TYPE_CHECKING import. THE HALF THAT MATTERS for a gate wedged at 'fail' - with this gate in `make verify`, a false red blocks every merge in the repository. The anchor must AGREE here or it differs for reasons beyond the blindness under test.

cases.name: good-allowed-accounted
cases.why: One undeclared module-level import, fully accounted for by a ledger line. Proves the ACCEPT path is live: no bad case can, because a gate ignoring the ledger entirely still scores every bad case BAD. Without this the accept path could be dead code with a full green board.

anchors.why: CONSTRUCTED, not historical, and PERMANENTLY so - ADR 0008's rule for a gate introduced by its own pull request: there is no blind ancestor of this gate on main, the anchor commit dies with the squash, and `--verify-provenance` therefore reads `unverified` forever rather than 'git is absent here'. Integrity rests on the sha256 above; historicity is not claimed. WHAT IT IS: the plausible FIRST CUT, not a strawman. It shares the real gate's population, stdlib screen and first-party screen, so it differs in exactly two places and the demonstration is isolated. Blindness 1: the declaration test is `name in pyproject_text`, which reports #1041's own tree clean because `types-requests` contains `requests`. Blindness 2: it reads the ledger and accepts what the lines name, but never asks whether a line accounts for anything. It prints `UNDECLARED-IMPORT:` on the findings it DOES make, so an anchor that unexpectedly caught a known-bad input scores INERT rather than UNRESOLVED (#946).
